title: 0/1 Knapsack
description:
A knapsack can carry a total weight of at most W. There are several items, each with a value and a weight. Every item is either taken whole or left behind: it cannot be split, and it cannot be taken more than once.

Implement a function called Knapsack that receives the capacity W, a list of item values and a list of item weights (position i of both lists describes the same item), and returns the largest total value of a set of items whose weights add up to no more than W.

Knapsack(W: 4, values: [1, 2, 3], weights: [4, 5, 1]) -> 3. The items of weight 4 and 1 each fit alone, but not together; the item of weight 1 alone is worth the most.
Knapsack(W: 3, values: [1, 2, 3], weights: [4, 5, 6]) -> 0. Nothing fits.
Knapsack(W: 50, values: [60, 100, 120], weights: [10, 20, 30]) -> 220. Taking the item with the best value per unit of weight first does not give the answer.

An item may only be counted once even when it would fit several times: Knapsack(W: 10, values: [10], weights: [3]) -> 10, not 30. With no items, or with a capacity of 0, the answer is 0.

The solution has to run in time proportional to the number of items times W, and use extra memory proportional to W alone. The hidden tests check this with 2000 items and a capacity of 10000, where a table with a row for every item would be far over the memory budget.
objective: Find the best value that fits in a knapsack when each item is taken whole or not at all, using memory proportional to the capacity.
